idiom_name: System.Func / System.Action / System.Comparison<T> stored by the context
implementation_notes: A delegate is the language's built-in single-method strategy, and the framework already ships the delegate types to use - Func<T,TResult>, Action<T>, Predicate<T>, Comparison<T>, Converter<TInput,TOutput> - so new delegate declarations are almost never needed (Microsoft's delegate design guidance says to reuse them). The context stores the delegate (or a settable property) and the caller passes a method group or a lambda; List<T>.Sort(Comparison<T>) is the framework's own strategy-taking API. Keep the interface form (second variant) when the strategy carries configuration with invariants, exposes several operations, or should be a named type that DI can resolve and tests can implement.
pitfalls: Delegates combine into multicast chains: using += (or an event) for what should be one strategy makes every attached method run, and each one sees the same arguments - use a plain property or field for a single strategy.
An unset delegate is null and invoking it throws NullReferenceException; use the null-conditional invocation (_pricing?.Invoke(...)) or assign a non-null default.
If one method on an invocation list throws, the remaining methods are not invoked; a chain must not be mistaken for a set of independent strategies unless failures are handled per handler.

variants.name: Interface with implementing classes (stateful or multi-operation strategies)
variants.idiom_name: IPricingStrategy implemented per algorithm and injected into the context
variants.implementation_notes: The classic GoF shape in C#: an interface declaring the strategy operations plus one class per algorithm, with the context holding an instance - the right choice when the strategy carries configuration (a discount, a connection string, tuning parameters), exposes more than one operation, or must exist as a named type for DI registration and test doubles. The two forms compose: a class that implements the interface can still be reached through a Func<T,TResult> when only one operation is needed, and constructor injection (Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection) keeps the concrete class out of the context entirely.
pitfalls: Instantiating the concrete strategy inside the context (new WholesalePricing(...) in the constructor, or a static service locator) restores the coupling the pattern removed; take it as a constructor dependency.
A stateful or IDisposable strategy registered as a singleton is shared across every context and leaks state or resources; scope registrations deliberately (scoped/transient).
An interface with a single method adds ceremony over Func<T,TResult>; keep it only where the named contract buys something (several operations, DI registration, explicit test seams).
